newsitem.title: USA: Republicans said pressured to support Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Republicans said pressured to support Gingrich.

text.p: A key member of the House Ethics subcommittee investigating charges against Speaker Newt Gingrich said he and another member were pressured to speak out in support of Gingrich, who has admitted violating House ethics rules, Time magazine reported on Saturday.

Reps. Porter Goss of Florida and Steve Schiff of New Mexico, the two Republicans on the four-member ethics subcommittee issued a letter last week publicly supporting Gingrich in his bid for reelection as Speaker.
They said in their letter they knew of "no reason now, nor do we foresee any in the normal course of events in the future, why Newt Gingrich would be ineligible to serve as Speaker."

Time, in its latest issue, said it was "highly unusual" for members of the ethics committee to make such a statement while a case was still under investigation. But what was even more unusual was the way the letter originated, it said.
Schiff told Time he first heard of the letter when a staffer for a member of the Republican House leadership read him Goss's handwritten text over the phone and asked if he would join in signing it.

Schiff said the letter was prepared "in response to urgings" by Reps. Bill Paxon of New York and John Linder of Georgia, respectively the outgoing and incoming chairmen of the National Republican Congressional Committee, who had been pressing Republican House members for months to get behind Gingrich.

He said Paxon and Linder approached him and Goss to propose that they make public whatever they properly could from the investigation before the speakership vote "because they said their phones were ringing off the wall with respect to members calling and asking questions."

Paxon insisted that Schiff and Goss acted "on their own initiative" but declined to elaborate on what he said were "my private conversations with members" when asked whether he had urged them to release information to House Republicans, Time reported. Goss declined to commnent.

The vote on the speaker will take place on Tuesday as Congress reconvenes one day before the House Ethics Committee begins the last phase of the Gingrich investigation that will result in a recommendation to the full House on punishment.
Speculation has been that the committee will recommend a reprimand, a lesser punishment than expulsion or censure and one that would likely enable Gingrich to keep his post.

Gingrich on Dec. 21 agreed with the finding of the ethics subcommittee that he had given investigators false information and failed to ensure that he complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt donations for partisan purposes.
